title: A CIA tool called “Ghost Murmur”, pairing quantum magnetometry with AI, may have located downed F-15E officer “Dude 44 Bravo” in Iran before his rescue in April 2026; CBS later reports that unnamed CIA technology pinpointed him
summary: Two anonymous sources credit the CIA's Ghost Murmur, quantum sensing paired with AI, with locating a downed F-15E officer in Iran; CBS reports that CIA technology pinpointed him and names no tool.
account: The White House briefing of 6 April 2026 documents the rescue of the downed F-15E weapons systems officer in Iran. The official transcript also describes watching his suspected position with a camera from 40 miles away. That distance concerns the camera, and no source establishes a range for detecting a heartbeat. On 7 April the New York Post reported that two anonymous sources attributed the officer's location to a Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) tool called Ghost Murmur. They described quantum magnetic sensing combined with AI that separates a heartbeat signal from background noise. They attributed its development to Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works. Lockheed Martin declined to comment. In a telephone interview with the Post on 8 April, President Trump called the tool important to the rescue but supplied no technical explanation. The Post and Scientific American separately interviewed physicists who questioned the described capability. The official briefing does not name Ghost Murmur or establish an AI contribution. No public measurements or inspectable technical account establish that the claimed system located the officer. On 13 September 2026, 60 Minutes reported from its own interviews that the CIA used top-secret technology to pinpoint the officer's location. CBS did not name Ghost Murmur or say that the technology used AI. Admiral Brad Cooper told CBS that messages from the officer, including "I'm hurt, I'm moving", reached US forces. The officer said that he carried communication equipment and that he did not immediately use it. The documented outcome is one rescued airman; the claimed AI contribution remains unverified.
purpose: According to the Post's sources, the tool was built to find a human heartbeat at a distance. The uses are intelligence collection and personnel recovery, and it was tested on Black Hawk helicopters. Its stated purpose matches the use claimed.
system: 'Ghost Murmur': long-range quantum (nitrogen-vacancy diamond) magnetometry paired with AI software that isolates heartbeat signatures from background noise, as described by the NY Post's anonymous sources
developer: Lockheed Martin Skunk Works, per two NY Post sources; the company declined to comment
deployer: US Central Intelligence Agency, per the NY Post; the CIA and White House named no tool

display.answer: The claim about Ghost Murmur traces to two anonymous sources in the New York Post and to President Trump's telephone interview with the same paper. The White House transcript documents the rescue. The Post and Scientific American interviewed physicists separately. CBS reports from its own interviews with the officer and with officials.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Two anonymous sources credit the CIA's Ghost Murmur, quantum sensing paired with AI, with locating a downed F-15E officer in Iran; CBS reports that CIA technology pinpointed him and names no tool.
fields.account: The White House briefing of 6 April 2026 documents the rescue of the downed F-15E weapons systems officer in Iran. The official transcript also describes watching his suspected position with a camera from 40 miles away. That distance concerns the camera, and no source establishes a range for detecting a heartbeat. On 7 April the New York Post reported that two anonymous sources attributed the officer's location to a Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) tool called Ghost Murmur. They described quantum magnetic sensing combined with AI that separates a heartbeat signal from background noise. They attributed its development to Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works. Lockheed Martin declined to comment. In a telephone interview with the Post on 8 April, President Trump called the tool important to the rescue but supplied no technical explanation. The Post and Scientific American separately interviewed physicists who questioned the described capability. The official briefing does not name Ghost Murmur or establish an AI contribution. No public measurements or inspectable technical account establish that the claimed system located the officer. On 13 September 2026, 60 Minutes reported from its own interviews that the CIA used top-secret technology to pinpoint the officer's location. CBS did not name Ghost Murmur or say that the technology used AI. Admiral Brad Cooper told CBS that messages from the officer, including "I'm hurt, I'm moving", reached US forces. The officer said that he carried communication equipment and that he did not immediately use it. The documented outcome is one rescued airman; the claimed AI contribution remains unverified.
